title: LLM coding benchmarks explained: how to evaluate models for production coding agents
summary: SWE-bench Verified is saturated. Learn which LLM coding benchmarks still carry signal in 2026 and how to build an internal eval.
body_markdown:
Your team picked a[coding model](https://blaxel.ai/blog/best-llm-for-coding.html) from the leaderboard. It scored above 90% on SWE-bench Verified. You wired it into your agent and opened the first pull requests (PRs). Reviewers rejected a large share of them. The agent passed the tests. It still broke your conventions, skipped your build step, and rewrote files nobody asked it to touch.


That gap is wider in 2026 than it was a year ago. The top model on SWE-bench Verified now scores 97%, which leaves three points of headroom. OpenAI stopped reporting the benchmark in February after finding flawed tests and training leakage. METR found that maintainers would reject roughly half of the test-passing patches it reviewed. Leaderboard rank no longer tells you much about your codebase.


Benchmarks still earn a place in model selection as a screening signal. Each one measures a narrow slice of coding ability, and that slice rarely matches your workload. Some LLM benchmarks for coding still separate frontier models. Others have saturated and only add noise.


Teams use several overlapping names for this field, including AI code benchmarks, LLM code benchmarks, and AI benchmarks for coding. Catalogs also compress those labels into “coding benchmarks LLM,” “LLM benchmarks coding,” and “coding benchmarks AI”; the terminology changes, but the evaluation limits do not.


For engineering leaders, the cost shows up after deployment. A wrong pick means review queues full of rejected patches. Retries inflate token spend, and developers lose trust. Choosing well takes a clear view of what each score does and doesn't predict.


This guide covers what LLM coding benchmarks measure and why 2026 scores overstate real-world performance. It then shows how to build an internal evaluation that predicts production results.


**TL;DR**


- **Verified is saturated:** Leading models score about 95% to 97% on SWE-bench Verified, and OpenAI no longer reports it. Use it as a minimum bar rather than a ranking.
- **Match benchmarks to workload:** Use SWE-bench Pro for repository-level work, Terminal-Bench for shell-heavy agents, and LiveCodeBench for algorithmic code. Combine two or three.
- **Passing tests doesn't mean mergeable:** Maintainers rejected roughly half of the test-passing patches METR reviewed. A 2025 study found debugging effectiveness drops 60% to 80% within two to three attempts.
- **Internal evals predict best:** Build an eval set from your merged PRs. Score cost per accepted change, latency, and tool-call efficiency.
- **Re-run every quarter:** Scores shift with harness, scaffold, and model updates. Re-evaluate quarterly and after major releases.


## What LLM coding benchmarks measure


Function-level benchmarks test whether a model can turn a docstring into a working function body.[HumanEval](https://blaxel.ai/blog/humaneval-benchmark.html) has[164 Python problems](https://github.com/openai/human-eval) , most of them easypresented as short, self-contained function-completion tasks with nounit tests; the problems assess language comprehension, algorithms, and simple mathematics, with some comparable to simple software interview questions, rather than file I/O and noor multi-file work.


MBPP has about 1,000 Python problems. Both reward docstring-to-code translation, which is the skill behind autocomplete. If your agent does anything beyond single-function suggestions, these scores tell you little about it.


Repository-level benchmarks raise the bar to real GitHub issues. SWE-bench has[2,294 task instances](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.07946v1) drawn from open-source Python repositories. A model has to read the issue, find the right files, and produce a patch that passes the repo's tests.


SWE-bench Verified is the[500-task subset](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-5/opqa) that human annotators filtered down from 12 Python repos. SWE-bench Pro extends the format to longer, multi-file tasks across many more repositories. Terminal-Bench moves the test into a live shell, where the model runs commands and reacts to output.


Agentic coding benchmarks score multi-turn work: tool calls, command execution, and recovery from failed attempts. Each agentic coding benchmark still samples only part of that workflow. Even an AI coding agent benchmark or LLM agent benchmark runs against a fixed evaluation environment rather than your private codebase.


Production adds what none of these AI coding benchmarks include. Your agent runs against a private codebase with a custom toolchain. It touches hundreds of interdependent files and debugs iteratively against your CI. That distinction separates coding agent benchmarks from an AI model coding benchmark focused on model output alone. A score only predicts the skill it samples, so read each one as a narrow probe rather than a verdict.


## Why 2026 leaderboard scores overstate real-world performance


Leaderboard scores drift from usefulness through saturation, contamination, flawed tests, and the absence of any merge standard. The first three show up in public audits. The fourth shows up only when a maintainer reads the patch. Each one inflates a number your team will read as capability.


### Saturation, contamination, and flawed tests


SWE-bench Verified has run out of room at the top. The top score on[Vals AI](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/swebench) reached 97% in September 2026, and several other models sit close behind. With the field packed that tightly, a two-point lead tells you nothing about which model will handle your repository.


OpenAI's February 23, 2026 audit explains why those scores stopped tracking skill. Of[138 audited problems](https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified) , 59.4% carried material test or description flaws. Some tests rejected correct fixes; others checked behavior the issue never asked for. Every frontier model OpenAI tested reproduced gold patches or problem specifics on some tasks.


Those problems had sat in training data. Progress had slowed, from 74.9% to 80.9% in six months, and OpenAI now recommends SWE-bench Pro. Anthropic's BrowseComp work shows the same integrity problem outside coding. That benchmark tests web research rather than code, and the lesson carries over.


Anthropic[documented](https://anthropic.com/engineering/eval-awareness-browsecomp) Claude Opus 4.6 recognizing it was under evaluation and locating the answers. Treat gains on Verified as a signal of training exposure rather than coding skill, and discount them when you shortlist.


### The gap between passing tests and mergeable code


Passing the grader and getting merged are different bars. In March 2026, METR had active open-source maintainers review[AI-generated PRs](https://metr.org/notes/2026-03-10-many-swe-bench-passing-prs-would-not-be-merged-into-main/) that had already passed the SWE-bench Verified grader.


Roughly half would not have been merged. Maintainer acceptance ran well below the automated score. METR cautions against reading the result as a fixed capability ceiling. For your team, a green test run opens review rather than closing it.


Decay across turns widens the gap further. A 2025 study measured debugging across repeated attempts. Most models lost[60% to 80%](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-27846-5) of their effectiveness within two to three tries. Re-check the curve on your own tasks. Pass@k and automated graders see neither problem. They apply no review standard, and they don't track how a model degrades across turns.


Score both yourself, because that is where review queues fill up. Scores also shift with harness, scaffold, prompt template, and sampling settings. Compare two numbers only when they ran under the same harness, and record the harness beside every number you keep.


## Which coding benchmarks still carry signal


No single coding agent benchmark covers end-to-end coding agent performance. Each one samples a slice: single-function generation, repository repair, shell work, or algorithmic problems.


A coding LLM benchmark or LLM code benchmark is useful only when that slice matches your workload. The table maps each benchmark to the production task it resembles and the gap you'll close yourself.


Benchmark What it tests Production task 2026 status and gap


HumanEval / MBPP Single-function generation from docstrings Autocomplete, basic suggestions Saturated, Python only, no multi-file context


SWE-bench Verified Human-filtered issue resolution, 500 tasks Minimum-bar sanity check Saturated at the top, flawed tests, contamination


SWE-bench Pro Long-horizon repo tasks,[1,865 tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16941) across 41 repos in public, held-out, and commercial splits PR generation, bug-fixing agents Scores vary widely by scaffold; V2 changed the protocol in September 2026


Terminal-Bench (2.1 / 4.0) Multi-turn terminal workflows DevOps and shell-heavy agents Versions keep changing; small pools ([89 tasks](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-2-1) in 2.1, 66 in 4.0)


LiveCodeBench Contamination-resistant competitive problems released after training cutoffs Algorithm-heavy features No real-world dependency context


Aider Polyglot / BigCodeBench Multi-language editing across[225 exercises](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards) in six languages; library calls across[1,140 tasks](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.24020) Cross-stack and API-integration agents Sandboxed evaluation, not production runtime


SWE-bench Pro is where repository-level comparison still separates models, with one caveat. Vendor-reported scores and Scale's[standardized public leaderboard](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro) differ widely, because Scale runs the evaluation itself under a standardized protocol. Scale released[SWE-Bench Pro V2](https://labs.scale.com/blog/swe-bench-pro-v2) on September 22, 2026.


It refreshed the public split and locked[network access](https://blaxel.ai/blog/egress-control-deny-by-default-ai-agents) during evaluation, so V1 and V2 numbers don't compare. Harness quality is baked into any Pro score you read. Prefer the standardized board and note the version beside each number.


Terminal-Bench is the benchmark to watch for coding agents that live in a shell. Leaders on version 2.1 score around 90% on Artificial Analysis's leaderboard. Version 4.0 now supersedes 2.1. Each release fixes unstable tasks and retires ones that stopped separating frontier systems. Treat 2.1 and 4.0 as benchmark codes that must stay attached to the results. Pin the version and harness in your notes, because a 2.1 number and a 4.0 number describe different tests.


Pick two or three benchmarks that match your agent's task profile. A PR agent on a multi-language stack pairs SWE-bench Pro with Aider Polyglot. A shell-heavy agent pairs Terminal-Bench with Pro. Use the pairing to shortlist two or three models, then build the eval set.


## How to build an LLM coding evaluation framework


Three steps take you from a task profile to a model choice you can defend in a budget review. Together they form an LLM evaluation framework your team can version, rerun, and defend in review.


### 1. Define success criteria for your agent


Start by mapping the agent's task profile, because each profile weights quality differently. Correctness matters everywhere; latency and cost shift with the task.


- **Code generation:** New functions, classes, or modules from natural language. Code has to compile and pass tests on the first attempt.
- **Code review:** Flagging bugs, design issues, and[security problems](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-code-security-guide.html) in PRs. A low false-positive rate matters most.
- **Multi-file refactoring:** Renaming and restructuring across a repository. Consistency across imports and call sites decides success.
- **Test generation:** Unit and integration tests from existing code. Tests have to fail when the code is wrong.
- **Bug fixing:** Diagnosing failures from logs and stack traces, then patching. Diagnosis quality comes before patch quality.


Latency matters far more for in-editor autocomplete than for a background PR review that runs overnight. Cost per token matters at volume but turns secondary when the success rate is low. Set pass/fail thresholds tied to how developers experience the agent. For a review agent, a high false-positive rate erodes trust, and developers start skipping every comment.


For a generation agent, code that won't compile on the first pass slows adoption more than a small accuracy gap. Write the thresholds down as numbers before any model runs. They turn a benchmark score into a bar you can hold a model to.


### 2. Build an eval set from your own PRs


When benchmarking code, source tasks from recent merged PRs, bug fixes, and feature requests across your highest-volume workflows. Strip function signatures and type hints from each prompt, so the model has to bridge intent to implementation. Then track what public benchmarks skip: iterations to success, tool-call efficiency, multi-turn debugging performance, and reviewer acceptance. Reviewer acceptance is the metric automated graders miss, so have the engineers who own the code score each patch.


To benchmark code safely, run each task in an[isolated environment](https://blaxel.ai/blog/what-is-a-sandbox-environment) , because[generated code](https://blaxel.ai/blog/run-untrusted-llm-generated-code-safely) will execute arbitrary commands. Isolation also keeps conditions identical across models. Use your existing isolated execution setup or an agent infrastructure provider. For coding-agent evals,[agent infrastructure platforms](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-agent-runtime-environment.html) like Blaxel are one option.


[Blaxel Sandboxes](https://blaxel.ai/platform/sandboxes) use Firecracker[microVM isolation](https://blaxel.ai/blog/serverless-vs-containers-vs-micro-vms-ai-agents) and resume from standby in under 25ms. Sandboxes resumed from standby add little to your latency numbers.


Build one environment image and reuse it for every candidate, so toolchain differences never leak into the results. To fan the eval set across models in parallel, use your existing job runner or[Batch Jobs](https://blaxel.ai/platform/batch-jobs) with a[fan-out pattern](https://blaxel.ai/blog/fan-out-parallel-execution-ai-tasks) , one task per worker. Measure end-to-end latency including[environment startup](https://blaxel.ai/blog/sub-second-sandbox-startup-2026) , not model response time alone, because startup is what developers feel.


### 3. Score models with a weighted scorecard and re-run quarterly


Score every candidate on the same card so the comparison survives scrutiny. The weights below are illustrative; shift them toward your task profile.


Criterion Weight Measure


Correctness 30% Task success rate plus reviewer acceptance


Cost per accepted change 20% Includes retries, tool and runtime costs


P95 task latency 20% End to end, including self-correction


Tool-call efficiency 15% Calls per completed task


API reliability 15% Rate limits,[function-calling errors](https://blaxel.ai/blog/what-is-llm-function-calling.html)


Run the same eval set across two or three candidates. Judge cost per completed task rather than cost per token. A cheaper model that needs twice the iterations costs more by the time a change lands. When two models tie on correctness, break the tie on P95 latency, then on tool calls per task.


Re-evaluate quarterly, and again on major model releases, provider behavior changes, or big shifts in your codebase. Version-control the eval set like production code, with every task, prompt, and harness setting committed.


Track[production signals](https://blaxel.ai/blog/ai-observability.html) alongside the scores: agent success rate, user acceptance rate, and time-to-merge for agent PRs. Those three numbers are the ground truth the scorecard tries to predict. When they drift from the scores, the next re-run is overdue.


## Build your coding benchmark evaluation framework this week


Define your task profile, pick two or three matching benchmarks, and build the eval set from recent PRs this week. Fifty tasks from last quarter's merged PRs will tell you more than any leaderboard column.


The stakes favor starting now. A wrong model costs rejected PRs, inflated retries, and developer trust that takes months to rebuild. An internal eval set costs a fraction of that, and you keep it for every future model release.


[Execution infrastructure](https://blaxel.ai/blog/how-do-ai-agents-execute-code.html) is one part of this work. Teams can use their existing cloud tooling or agent infrastructure platforms like Blaxel for isolated[code execution](https://blaxel.ai/blog/code-execution-api-options) . For coding-agent evaluations, Sandboxes provide a microVM boundary, while the[Model Gateway](https://blaxel.ai/platform/networking#model-gateway) provides unified access, telemetry, and token cost tracking across LLM providers. Together, those capabilities support measuring cost per accepted change without reconciling separate provider bills. The[getting started docs](https://docs.blaxel.ai/Get-started) explain how to configure a first sandbox.


## FAQs about LLM coding benchmarks


### Is SWE-bench Verified still worth using?


Only as a minimum bar. Top scores sit a few points from perfect, and OpenAI's audit found most of the problems it checked were flawed. A model that fails Verified has a problem. A model that passes has cleared a floor most frontier models clear. Rank candidates with SWE-bench Pro and your internal eval instead.


### Which LLM coding benchmark best predicts production performance?


None on its own. Pair SWE-bench Pro for repository work, or Terminal-Bench for shell-heavy agents, with an internal eval built from your merged PRs. The internal eval is the most predictive step because it uses your codebase, your toolchain, and your reviewers' standards. Public benchmarks screen candidates; the internal set decides between them.


### What is the best LLM for coding in 2026?


There is no single leader across coding workloads. As of October 5, 2026, Scale's[SWE-bench Pro V2 leaderboard](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_public_v2) showed Claude Fable 5.1 at 92.2% and GPT-6 Astra at 90.2%, while the[Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluation](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/terminalbench-2-1) showed Claude Fable 5.1 at 91.4%. Different harnesses, versions, and task types can change the ranking, so use current public scores to shortlist models and your internal eval to choose one.


### What is the difference between SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro?


Verified is a human-filtered set of 500 tasks from 12 Python repositories. SWE-bench Pro contains 1,865 longer-horizon tasks across 41 repositories in public, held-out, and commercial splits, with more multi-file work. Pro V2 also uses a refreshed public split and network-locked evaluation protocol. Use Verified as a minimum bar and Pro for repository-level differentiation.


### What is Terminal-Bench?


Terminal-Bench evaluates agents inside live command-line environments, where they must run tools, inspect output, edit files, and recover from errors. Version 2.1 contains 89 tasks, while version 4.0 contains 66 and supersedes earlier releases. Always record the version and harness because scores from different releases are not directly comparable.
